arXiv:2206.08602v1 [math.AP] 17 Jun 2022

Large-time asymptotic behaviors for the classical thermoelastic system

Wenhui Chen ††thanks: Wenhui Chen (wenhui.chen.math@gmail.com) Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Information Science, Guangzhou University, 510006 Guangzhou, China    Hiroshi Takeda ††thanks: Hiroshi Takeda (h-takeda@fit.ac.jp) Affiliation: Department of Intelligent Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Fukuoka Institute of Technology, 811-0295 Fukuoka, Japan
Abstract

In this paper, we study the classical thermoelastic system with Fourier’s law of heat conduction in the whole space ℝ⋉\mathbb{R}^{n} when n=1,2,3n=1,2,3, particularly, asymptotic profiles for its elastic displacement as large-time. We discover optimal growth estimates of the elastic displacement when n=1,2n=1,2, whose growth rates coincide with those for the free wave model, whereas when n=3n=3 the optimal decay rate is related to the Gaussian kernel. Furthermore, under a new condition for weighted datum, the large-time optimal leading term is firstly introduced by the combination of diffusion-waves, the heat kernel and singular components. We also illustrate a second-order profile of solution by diffusion-waves with weighted L1L^{1} datum as a by-product. These results imply that wave-structure large-time behaviors hold only for the one- and two-dimensional thermoelastic systems.

Keywords: thermoelastic system, Fourier’s law, optimal estimate, optimal leading term, asymptotic profile, diffusion-waves.

AMS Classification (2020) 35G40, 35B40, 35Q79

1 Introduction

It is well-known that the reciprocal actions between elastic stresses and thermal behaviors including temperature difference of an elastic heat conductive media are effectively described by the thermoelastic systems mathematically (see [1, 4, 11] and references therein). The classical model of thermoelasticity (see an extensive review [1]) is constructed by an elasticity, e.g. the isotropic elastic waves, coupled with Fourier’s law of heat conduction

q=−κ∇θ\displaystyle{q}=-\kappa\nabla\theta

with the heat flux q=q⁡(t,x)∈ℝ⋉{q}={q}(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and the temperature (relative to some reference temperature) θ=θ⁡(t,x)∈ℝ\theta=\theta(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}, where the positive constant κ\kappa denotes the thermal conductivity. In other words, the classical thermoelastic model is a hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system. Let us consider the Cauchy problem for the classical thermoelastic system in the physical dimensions n=1,2,3n=1,2,3, namely,

{ut​t−a2Δu−(b2−a2)∇divu+γ1∇θ=0,θt−κ​Δ​θ+γ2​div⁡ut=0,u(0,x)=u0(x),ut(0,x)=u1(x),θ(0,x)=θ0(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{tt}-a^{2}\Delta u-(b^{2}-a^{2})\nabla\divv u+\gamma_{1}\nabla\theta=0,\\ \theta_{t}-\kappa\Delta\theta+\gamma_{2}\divv u_{t}=0,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\ u_{t}(0,x)=u_{1}(x),\ \theta(0,x)=\theta_{0}(x),\end{cases} (1)

with (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ⋉(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}, where two unknowns u=u⁡(t,x)∈ℝ⋉u=u(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and θ=θ⁡(t,x)∈ℝ\theta=\theta(t,x)\in\mathbb{R} stand for the elastic displacement and the temperature difference to the equilibrium state, respectively. The speeds for propagation of the longitudinal P-wave and of the transverse S-wave are denoted by bb and aa, individually, fulfilling b>a>0b>a>0, whose combinations a2a^{2} and b2−2​a2b^{2}-2a^{2} are the well-known Lamé constants. Some physical properties of the underlying isotropic medium for (1) are described by the thermal conductivity κ>0\kappa>0 and the thermoelastic coupling coefficients γ1,γ2\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2} such that γ1​γ2>0\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}>0.

We recall now some historical background to the classical thermoelasticity

{ut​t−a2Δu−(b2−a2)∇divu+γ1∇θ=0,θt−κ​Δ​θ+γ2​div⁡ut=0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{tt}-a^{2}\Delta u-(b^{2}-a^{2})\nabla\divv u+\gamma_{1}\nabla\theta=0,\\ \theta_{t}-\kappa\Delta\theta+\gamma_{2}\divv u_{t}=0.\end{cases} (2)

Actually, the theory of thermoelasticity is very classical and was first founded by J.M.C. Duhamel, K.E. Neumann and W. Thomson, etc. in 18th century. Therewith, the pioneering paper [13] applied the classical thermodynamics methods to deduce the coupled system of thermoelasticity. In the homogeneous and isotropic medium with vanishing external body forces as well as heats, the classical thermoelastic system (2) can be derived in general. In recent thirty years, the classical thermoelastic systems (2) in bounded or unbounded domains have caught a lot of attentions (see [3, 18, 19, 20, 23, 15, 16, 24, 25, 11, 28, 9, 10] and references therein). According to the theme of this work, we just briefly introduce the progressive progress in the corresponding Cauchy problem (1). By employing the Helmholtz decomposition, the solution may be split into

u=up0+us0,u=u^{p_{0}}+u^{s_{0}},

where the solenoidal part us0u^{s_{0}} solves the well-studied wave equation (see (7) soon afterwards) and the potential part up0u^{p_{0}} fulfills

{up0t​t−b2Δup0+γ1∇θ=0,θt−κ​Δ​θ+γ2​div⁡utp0=0,up0(0,x)=u0p0(x),up0t(0,x)=u1p0(x),θ(0,x)=θ0(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}u^{p_{0}}_{tt}-b^{2}\Delta u^{p_{0}}+\gamma_{1}\nabla\theta=0,\\ \theta_{t}-\kappa\Delta\theta+\gamma_{2}\divv u^{p_{0}}_{t}=0,\\ u^{p_{0}}(0,x)=u_{0}^{p_{0}}(x),\ u^{p_{0}}_{t}(0,x)=u_{1}^{p_{0}}(x),\ \theta(0,x)=\theta_{0}(x),\end{cases} (3)

carrying rot⁡up0=0\rott u^{p_{0}}=0 with (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ⋉(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3. The authors of [11] constructed the standard energy (b​div⁡up0,utp0,θ)∈ℝ⋉+⊭(b\divv u^{p_{0}},u^{p_{0}}_{t},\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+2} and employed energy methods for the first-order coupled system associated with anti-symmetric properties of coefficient matrix to derive

‖(b​div⁡up0,utp0,θ)​(t,⋅)‖(L2)n+2≲(1+t)−n4​‖(b​div⁡u0p0,u1p0,θ0)‖(L2∩L1)n+2.\displaystyle\|(b\divv u^{p_{0}},u^{p_{0}}_{t},\theta)(t,\cdot)\|_{(L^{2})^{n+2}}\lesssim(1+t)^{-\frac{n}{4}}\|(b\divv u^{p_{0}}_{0},u^{p_{0}}_{1},\theta_{0})\|_{(L^{2}\cap L^{1})^{n+2}}. (4)

Later, the paper [9] applied the so-called diagonalization procedure (it may decouple the system and search for the dominant parts of vector unknown in local zones) for a suitable micro-energy (utp0±i​b​|D|​up0,θ)(u^{p_{0}}_{t}\pm ib|D|u^{p_{0}},\theta) in which the operator |D||D| owns the symbol |ξ||\xi|. Applying WKB analysis and multi-steps diagonalization method, the authors derived L2L^{2} well-posedness, propagation of singularities, Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} decay estimates and parabolic-type diffusion phenomenon. Particularly, the (L2∩L1)−L2(L^{2}\cap L^{1})-L^{2} estimate conforms to the same decay rate as the one in (4). For these reasons, in the framework of energy unknowns, the thermoelastic system (3) has parabolic-type decay properties whose decay rate comes from the Gaussian kernel ℱξ→x−1​(e−c​|ξ|2​t)\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}(\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}).

As we mentioned in the above, there are a lot of related works begun from the past century in terms of the classical thermoelasticity (1). Some suitable energy terms, e.g. the standard energy (b​div⁡up0,utp0,θ)(b\divv u^{p_{0}},u_{t}^{p_{0}},\theta) in [11, Equation (4.65)], decay polynomially with parabolic-type in the L2L^{2} framework, and some asymptotic profiles of these energy terms fulfill parabolic-structure reference systems, e.g. diffusion phenomena stated in [9]. Consequently, some natural questions are:

  • •

    Whether or not one can describe more detailed information of the elastic displacement uu or up0u^{p_{0}} for large-time?

  • •

    How does the elastic waves part influence on the large-time behaviors?

It will play a crucial role when a model equips some nonlinear terms containing uu itself, for instance, [24, 25, 12, 17] considered the nonlinear source term 𝒩⁡(u)\mathcal{N}(u) appearing on the first equation of (1). However, to the best of knowledge of authors, the optimal estimates and optimal leading terms of the elastic displacement in thermoelasticity are still open even for the irrotational situation. Here, the optimality is guaranteed by the same behaviors of upper bound and lower bound estimates for large-time (see, for example, [6, 8, 14] for the viscoelastic damped waves). We will partially give answers to the above questions by deep understanding of the effect of thermal damping generated by Fourier’s law.

The main purpose of this work is to study asymptotic behaviors of the potential part up0u^{p_{0}} to the Cauchy problem (3) because of the well-established properties for the solenoidal part us0u^{s_{0}}. Note that up0:=(u1,p0,⋯,un,p0)∈ℝ⋉u^{p_{0}}:=(u^{1,p_{0}},\cdots,u^{n,p_{0}})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with x∈ℝ⋉x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and uk,p0u^{k,p_{0}} is a element among them. By reducing the hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system to the third-order (in time) evolution equation with respect to uk,p0u^{k,p_{0}}, we employ WKB analysis and Fourier analysis to characterize the optimal large-time estimates

‖uk,p0​(t,⋅)‖L22≃{tifn=1,ln⁡tifn=2,t−12ifn=3,\displaystyle\|u^{k,p_{0}}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\simeq\begin{cases}t&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \ln t&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\\ t^{-\frac{1}{2}}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=3,\end{cases}

with L1∩L2L^{1}\cap L^{2} datum if

|Pu1k,p0|+|Pθ0|≠0\displaystyle|P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}|+|P_{\theta_{0}}|\neq 0

carrying the mean Pf=∫ℝ⋉f⁡(x)​𝑑xP_{f}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x)\mathrm{d}x, where the solution grows polynomially when n=1n=1 and logarithmically when n=2n=2, but decay polynomially in higher-dimensions. Particularly, due to the identical growth rates for the thermoelastic system and the wave equation when n=1,2n=1,2, we claim the decisive part of the one- and two-dimensional thermoelastic system (1) is the waves part as t≫1t\gg 1, whereas Fourier’s law of heat conduction exerts crucial influence when n=3n=3 (see the detail explanation in Remark 2.4). This wave-type large-time behavior is the new discovery, and different from the parabolic-type decay properties in the previous literature of thermoelasticity. One of the main difficulties is to understand interplay among dissipative part, oscillating part and the singularity (as |ξ|→0|\xi|\to 0) for the next multiplier:

ℳn​(t,|ξ|):=1|ξ|​(e−β0​|ξ|2​t−cos⁡(β1​|ξ|​t)​e−β2​|ξ|2​t)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|):=\frac{1}{|\xi|}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{0}|\xi|^{2}t}-\cos(\beta_{1}|\xi|t)\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\right)

in the L2L^{2} norm, where the positive constants are

β0=κ​b2b2+γ1​γ2,β1=b2+γ1​γ2andβ2=κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2).\displaystyle\beta_{0}=\frac{\kappa b^{2}}{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}},\ \ \beta_{1}=\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \beta_{2}=\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}.

Furthermore, introducing the leading term φk=φk​(t,x)\varphi^{k}=\varphi^{k}(t,x) such that

φk:=ℱξ→x−1​(sin⁡(β1​|ξ|​t)β1​|ξ|​e−β2​|ξ|2​t)​Pu1k,p0−i​γ1β12​ℛk​ℱξ→x−1​[1|ξ|​(cos⁡(β1​|ξ|​t)​e−β2​|ξ|2​t−e−β0​|ξ|2​t)]​Pθ0\displaystyle\varphi^{k}:=\mathcal{F}_{\xi\to x}^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin(\beta_{1}|\xi|t)}{\beta_{1}|\xi|}\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\right)P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}-\frac{i\gamma_{1}}{\beta_{1}^{2}}\mathcal{R}_{k}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}\left[\frac{1}{|\xi|}\left(\cos(\beta_{1}|\xi|t)\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{0}|\xi|^{2}t}\right)\right]P_{\theta_{0}}

with the Riesz transform ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k}, we derive the optimal decay estimates of the error term

‖uk,p0​(t,⋅)−φk​(t,⋅)‖L22≃t−n2\displaystyle\|u^{k,p_{0}}(t,\cdot)-\varphi^{k}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\simeq t^{-\frac{n}{2}}

for t≫1t\gg 1 and n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 if

|Pu0k,p0|+|Pu1k,p0|+|Pθ0|+|Mu1k,p0|+|Mθ0|≠0\displaystyle|P_{u_{0}^{k,p_{0}}}|+|P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}|+|P_{\theta_{0}}|+|M_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}|+|M_{\theta_{0}}|\neq 0

carrying the weighted mean Mf=∫ℝ⋉x​f​(x)​𝑑xM_{f}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}xf(x)\mathrm{d}x. That is to say that the function φk​(t,x)\varphi^{k}(t,x), which is the combination of diffusion-waves and heat kernel with the singular component (for small frequencies), is the optimal leading term for the thermoelastic system. As a by-product, we also investigate a second-order asymptotic profile of solution via higher-order diffusive-waves and heat model in the L2L^{2} framework. To sum up, novel first- and second-order asymptotic profiles for large-time characterized by diffusion-waves (instead of parabolic structure reference systems in the previous researches) for the thermoelastic system are discovered.

To end this paper, we state some concluding remarks related to other models of thermoelasticity in Section 5, and a new proof of optimal growth estimates for the free wave equation in Appendix A, which improves the assumption of initial datum in [7, Theorems 1.1, and 1.2].

2 Main results

2.1 Pretreatments by the Helmholtz decomposition

Before stating the main results of this work, let us simplify the model (1) and turn to our essential target hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system (3), in which the one-dimensional case can be trivially got without using this approach. According to the Helmholtz decomposition

L2=∇H1¯⊕𝒟0forn=2,3,\displaystyle L^{2}=\overline{\nabla H^{1}}\oplus\mathcal{D}_{0}\ \ \mbox{for}\ \ n=2,3,

with the function spaces

∇H1\displaystyle\nabla H^{1} :={∇ψ|ψ∈H1},\displaystyle:=\left\{\nabla\psi\ |\ \psi\in H^{1}\right\},
𝒟0\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0} :={u∈L2|(∇ϕ,u)L2=0with∀ϕ∈𝒞0∞},\displaystyle:=\left\{u\in L^{2}\ |\ (\nabla\phi,u)_{L^{2}}=0\ \ \mbox{with}\ \ \forall\phi\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}\right\},

and thus by such technique the solution u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) to (1) can be decomposed into a potential part and a solenoidal part such that

u=up0+us0.\displaystyle u=u^{p_{0}}+u^{s_{0}}. (6)

Here, the vector up0=up0​(t,x)u^{p_{0}}=u^{p_{0}}(t,x) is rotation-free and us0=us0​(t,x)u^{s_{0}}=u^{s_{0}}(t,x) is divergence-free in a weak sense. We clarify the nomenclature: the potential solution by the unknown up0u^{p_{0}} for the sake of briefness. Applying the identity

∇div⁡u=∇×(∇×u)+Δ​u\displaystyle\nabla\divv u=\nabla\times(\nabla\times u)+\Delta u

in two- and three-dimensions, we are able to decompose (1) into the wave model

{ut​ts0−a2​Δ​us0=0,us0(0,x)=us00(x),us0t(0,x)=us01(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}u^{s_{0}}_{tt}-a^{2}\Delta u^{s_{0}}=0,\\ u^{s_{0}}(0,x)=u^{s_{0}}_{0}(x),\ u^{s_{0}}_{t}(0,x)=u^{s_{0}}_{1}(x),\end{cases} (7)

and the hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system (3) with (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ⋉(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}, under the conditions div⁡us0=0\divv u^{s_{0}}=0 as well as rot⁡up0=0\rott u^{p_{0}}=0. Although the last treatment were considered when n=2,3n=2,3, one may notice that the one-dimensional coupled system (1) is exactly the same as the coupled system (3) when n=1n=1. Therefore, in the one-dimensional case, we may understand u=up0u=u^{p_{0}}.

The studies for linear wave equation (7) are well-known, for example, the author of [7, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2] stated the optimal estimates for the weighted L1L^{1} data, or the improved result in Corollary A.1 requiring L1L^{1} regularity only for the second data. Again, our main task in this paper, consequently, will be immediately turned into:

Asymptotic behaviors for the hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system (3) when n=1,2,3n=1,2,3.

Particularly, large-time asymptotic profiles including some optimal estimates, optimal leading terms as well as second-order approximations for the potential solution up0u^{p_{0}} with some weighted L1L^{1} datum are of interest.

Remark 2.1.

After obtaining some qualitative properties of solutions to (3) and referring those for the wave equation (7), we may claim the desired properties for the original thermoealstic system (1) in two- and three-dimensions according to the relation (6). Straightforwardly, due to rot⁡u≡0\rott u\equiv 0 when x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, our results for the coupled system (3) exactly coincide with those for the original system (1) when n=1n=1.

Remark 2.2.

If one considers the irrotational thermoelastic system (for instance, [22, Sections 3 and 4]) that is (1) carrying rot⁡u≡0\rott u\equiv 0, then the irrotational system will turn into (3), and all results in this paper immediately work for u=(u1,⋯,un)u=(u^{1},\cdots,u^{n}) with n=1,2,3n=1,2,3.

2.2 Main result on optimal estimates of the potential solution

Let us state the first result in this paper concerning L2L^{2} optimal estimates of each element of the potential solution up0u^{p_{0}}, particularly, it implies infinite time L2L^{2}-blowup of solution when n=1,2n=1,2. However, the solution will decay polynomially when n=3n=3.

Theorem 2.1.

Let us consider the hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system (3) for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 carrying initial datum u0k,p0,u1k,p0,θ0∈L2∩L1u^{k,p_{0}}_{0},u^{k,p_{0}}_{1},\theta_{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{1} with k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n. Then, the elastic displacement uk,p0u^{k,p_{0}} satisfies the following optimal estimates:

𝒜n(t)|𝔸|≲∥≊ℸ,∣⊬(≈,⋅)∥𝕃⊭≲𝔸⋉(≈)‖(≊⊬ℸ,∣⊬,≊⊮ℸ,∣⊬,θ⊬)‖(𝕃⊭∩𝕃⊮)⊯\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{n}(t)|\mathbb{A}|\lesssim\|u^{k,p_{0}}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\mathcal{A}_{n}(t)\left\|\left(u_{0}^{k,p_{0}},u_{1}^{k,p_{0}},\theta_{0}\right)\right\|_{(L^{2}\cap L^{1})^{3}} (8)

for t≫1t\gg 1, where the time-dependent coefficient 𝒜n​(t)\mathcal{A}_{n}(t) was defined in (5), and the positive constant on the left-hand side is defined by

𝔸⊭:=|ℙ≊⊮ℸ,∣⊬|⊭+|ℙθ⊬|⊭.\displaystyle\mathbb{A}^{2}:=|P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}|^{2}+|P_{\theta_{0}}|^{2}. (9)

Namely, provided that |𝔸|≠⊬|\mathbb{A}|\neq 0, then the optimal estimates ‖uk,p0​(t,⋅)‖L2≃𝒜n​(t)\|u^{k,p_{0}}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq\mathcal{A}_{n}(t) hold for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 and any t≫1t\gg 1.

Remark 2.3.

According to the relation

θ⁡(t,x)=−1i​γ1​ℱξ→x−1​[1ξk​(u^t​tk,p0​(t,ξ)+b2​|ξ|2​u^k,p0​(t,ξ))],\displaystyle\theta(t,x)=-\frac{1}{i\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}\left[\frac{1}{\xi_{k}}\left(\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{tt}(t,\xi)+b^{2}|\xi|^{2}\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}(t,\xi)\right)\right],

one may obtain optimal estimates for the temperature variable without any additional difficulty. Precisely, if u0k,p0∈H1∩L1u_{0}^{k,p_{0}}\in H^{1}\cap L^{1} and u1k,p0,θ0∈L2∩L1u_{1}^{k,p_{0}},\theta_{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{1} equipping |𝔸|≠⊬|\mathbb{A}|\neq 0 defined in (9), then the optimal decay estimates ‖θ⁡(t,⋅)‖L2≃t−n4\|\theta(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq t^{-\frac{n}{4}} hold for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 any any t≫1t\gg 1.

Remark 2.4.

Let us recall the large-time behavior of the free wave model

{wt​t−Δ​w=0,w(0,x)=w0(x),wt(0,x)=w1(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}w_{tt}-\Delta w=0,\\ w(0,x)=w_{0}(x),\ w_{t}(0,x)=w_{1}(x),\end{cases} (10)

with (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ⋉(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} for n=1,2n=1,2. Under (L2∩L1)×(L2∩L1,1)(L^{2}\cap L^{1})\times(L^{2}\cap L^{1,1}) regularity with |Pw1|≠0|P_{w_{1}}|\neq 0 assumption on initial datum, the recent work [7] got the optimal growth estimates

‖w⁡(t,⋅)‖L2≃{tifn=1,ln⁡tifn=2,\displaystyle\|w(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq\begin{cases}\sqrt{t}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \sqrt{\ln t}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\end{cases} (11)

for t≫1t\gg 1. Note that the weighted L1L^{1} regularity for the second data will be relaxed by L1L^{1} only in Corollary A.1 with the aid of a different idea. In Theorem 2.1, we indeed obtained the optimal estimates of the thermoelasticity (3) (or the wave equation (10) coupled with Fourier’s law of heat conduction) by the following one:

‖uk,p0​(t,⋅)‖L2≃{tifn=1,ln⁡tifn=2,t−14ifn=3,\displaystyle\|u^{k,p_{0}}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq\begin{cases}\sqrt{t}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \sqrt{\ln t}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\\ t^{-\frac{1}{4}}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=3,\end{cases}

for t≫1t\gg 1. We may notice that the growth rates for the free waves and the thermoelastic system are exactly the same if n=1,2n=1,2, but the solution decays polynomially with the aid of thermal dissipation generated by Fourier’s law. One may see Table 1 in detail.

It is worth noting that all large-time properties in Table 1 are optimal in the sense of same behaviors for upper bound and lower bound of the elastic displacement in the L2L^{2} norm. In particular, concerning n=1,2n=1,2, we may observe that the large-time properties of the thermoelastic system (3) are not influenced by the heat conduction. Analogously, this phenomenon is also valid for the classical thermoelastic system (1) due to the decomposition (6) and the fact that the wave solution us0u^{s_{0}} fulfills the estimates (11).

Remark 2.5.

One may find the growth/decay phenomena between the strong damping (or the so-called viscoelastic damping) and thermal dissipation from Fourier’s law on the wave model (10) are the same. Indeed, the authors of [6, 8] showed that the solution of strongly damped waves (i.e. the Cauchy problem for wt​t−Δ​w−Δ​wt=0w_{tt}-\Delta w-\Delta w_{t}=0) in the L2L^{2} norm satisfies the estimates with 𝒜n​(t)\mathcal{A}_{n}(t) to be optimal growth or decay rates. Importantly, Theorem 2.1 implies the same estimates of the thermoelastic system as those in the strongly damped waves.

One of our new observations is the optimal leading term φk​(t,x)\varphi^{k}(t,x) having diffusion-waves structure rather than parabolic structures for energy terms.     λ2,3\displaystyle\lambda_{2,3} =±i​b​|ξ|−γ1​γ22​κ+𝒪⁡(|ξ|−1).\displaystyle=\pm ib|\xi|-\frac{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2\kappa}+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{-1}).
  • •

    Concerning ξ∈𝒵bdd​(ε0,N0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\bdd}(\varepsilon_{0},N_{0}), the roots fulfill ℜ⁡λj<0\Re\lambda_{j}<0 for any j=1,2,3j=1,2,3.

Remark 3.1.

Different from the usual asymptotic expansions for characteristic roots (no matter Taylor-like expansion method [5] or diagonalization procedure [9] in the coupled systems), we not only derived pairwise distinct value with negative real parts when ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), but also found further expansions of characteristic roots containing |ξ|3|\xi|^{3}- and |ξ|4|\xi|^{4}-terms in Proposition 3.1, which will be applied when we study higher-order profiles and optimal leading terms.

Due to the fact that the discriminant of the cubic (19) is strictly negative for ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), two complex (non-real) roots λ2,3\lambda_{2,3} are conjugate, namely, λ2,3=λR±i​λI\lambda_{2,3}=\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\pm i\lambda_{\mathrm{I}} for small frequencies carrying the asymptotic expansions

λR=−κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2+𝒪⁡(|ξ|4),λI=b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|−κ2​γ1​γ2​(γ1​γ2+4​b2)8​(b2+γ1​γ2)5/2​|ξ|3+𝒪⁡(|ξ|4).\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}=-\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}|\xi|^{2}+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{4}),\ \ \lambda_{\mathrm{I}}=\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|-\frac{\kappa^{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}+4b^{2})}{8(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})^{5/2}}|\xi|^{3}+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{4}).

From the above setting, the solution u^k,p0=u^k,p0​(t,ξ)\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}=\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}(t,\xi) for ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}) owns the representation

u^k,p0\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}} =−(λI2+λR2)​u^0k,p0+2​λR​u^1k,p0−u^2k,p02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​eλ1​t+(2​λR​λ1−λ12)​u^0k,p0−2​λR​u^1k,p0+u^2k,p02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t\displaystyle=\frac{-(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2})\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}+2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{u}_{2}^{k,p_{0}}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}+\frac{(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{2})\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}-2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}+\widehat{u}_{2}^{k,p_{0}}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}
+λ1​(λR​λ1+λI2−λR2)​u^0k,p0+(λR2−λI2−λ12)​u^1k,p0−(λR−λ1)​u^2k,p0λI​(2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12)​sin⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t,\displaystyle\quad+\frac{\lambda_{1}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2})\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}+(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}-\lambda_{1})\widehat{u}_{2}^{k,p_{0}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t},

where the last data is fixed by u^2k,p0:=−b2​|ξ|2​u^0k,p0−i​γ1​ξk​θ^0\widehat{u}_{2}^{k,p_{0}}:=-b^{2}|\xi|^{2}\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{0}-i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}\widehat{\theta}_{0} with k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n. Let us reformulate the representation with the aid of the last data so that

u^k,p0\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}} =(b2​|ξ|2−λI2−λR2)​u^0k,p0+2​λR​u^1k,p0+i​γ1​ξk​θ^02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​eλ1​t\displaystyle=\frac{(b^{2}|\xi|^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2})\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}+2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}+i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}\widehat{\theta}_{0}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}
+(2​λR​λ1−λ12−b2​|ξ|2)​u^0k,p0−2​λR​u^1k,p0−i​γ1​ξk​θ^02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t\displaystyle\quad+\frac{(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{2}-b^{2}|\xi|^{2})\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}-2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}\widehat{\theta}_{0}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}
+[λ1​(λR​λ1+λI2−λR2)+b2​|ξ|2​(λR−λ1)]​u^0k,p0λI​(2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12)​sin⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t\displaystyle\quad+\frac{[\lambda_{1}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2})+b^{2}|\xi|^{2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}-\lambda_{1})]\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}
+(λR2−λI2−λ12)​u^1k,p0+i​γ1​ξk​(λR−λ1)​θ^0λI​(2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12)​sin⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t.\displaystyle\quad+\frac{(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}+i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}-\lambda_{1})\widehat{\theta}_{0}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}. (20)

We should underline that the formula (20) still holds for |ξ|⩾N0≫1|\xi|\geqslant N_{0}\gg 1, however, these components will be modified by

λR=−γ1​γ22​κ+𝒪⁡(|ξ|−1),λI=b​|ξ|+𝒪⁡(|ξ|−1),\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}=-\frac{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2\kappa}+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{-1}),\ \ \lambda_{\mathrm{I}}=b|\xi|+\mathcal{O}(|\xi|^{-1}),

since the strictly negative discriminant for ξ∈𝒵ext​(N0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\extt}(N_{0}).

3.3 Pointwise estimates and auxiliary functions in the Fourier space

The solution formula (20) still seems too complex to analyze its asymptotic behaviors. For this reason, we have to build several bridges by auxiliary functions. Indeed, as ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), we extract the dominant terms J^0k=J^0k​(t,ξ)\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}=\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}(t,\xi) such that

J^0k=−λI​sin⁡(λI​t)​u^1k,p02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​eλR​t+i​γ1​ξk​θ^02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​(eλ1​t−cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t),\displaystyle\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}=-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}+\frac{i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}\widehat{\theta}_{0}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}-\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}\right),

as well as the further one J^1k=J^1k​(t,ξ)\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}=\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}(t,\xi) according to

J^1k\displaystyle\widehat{J}_{1}^{k} :=(b2​|ξ|2−λI2)​eλ1​t−b2​|ξ|2​cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​u^0k,p0+2​λR​u^1k,p02​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​(eλ1​t−cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t)\displaystyle:=\frac{(b^{2}|\xi|^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2})\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}-b^{2}|\xi|^{2}\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}+\frac{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}-\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}\right)
+i​γ1​ξk​(λR−λ1)​θ^0λI​(2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12)​sin⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t.\displaystyle\ \ \quad+\frac{i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}-\lambda_{1})\widehat{\theta}_{0}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}.

Let us next propose some estimates for the above functions and the refined estimates of solutions by subtracting these functions.

Proposition 3.2.

Concerning ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), the following estimates for the auxiliary functions as well as the error terms hold:

χint​(ξ)​|J^0k|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}| ≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(t+|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)||ξ|)​(|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|),\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(\sqrt{t}+\frac{|\sin(|\xi|t)|}{|\xi|}\right)\left(|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right), (21)
χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}| ≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​[|u^0k,p0|+(1+t+|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)||ξ|)​(|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|)],\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left[|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+\left(1+\sqrt{t}+\frac{|\sin(|\xi|t)|}{|\xi|}\right)\left(|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right)\right],
χint​(ξ)​(|J^1k|+|u^k,p0−J^0k|)\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left(|\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}|+|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}|\right) ≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|),\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right), (22)
χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0−J^0k−J^1k|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}-\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}| ≲χint​(ξ)​|ξ|​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|),\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\xi|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|\right),

for any k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n.

Proof.

By using the next trick:

eλ1​t−cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t\displaystyle\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}-\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t} =(eλ1​t−eλR​t)+(1−cos⁡(λI​t))​eλR​t\displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}\right)+\big(1-\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\big)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}
=(λ1−λR)​t​eλR​t​∫01e(λ1−λR)​t​s​𝑑s+2​sin2⁡(12​λI​t)​eλR​t,\displaystyle=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}})t\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}})ts}\mathrm{d}s+2\sin^{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t\right)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}, (23)

and Proposition 3.1 for ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), we claim

χint​(ξ)​|J^0k|≲χint​(ξ)​|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)||ξ|​e−c​|ξ|2​t​|u^1k,p0|+χint​(ξ)​(|ξ|​t+|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|2|ξ|)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​|θ^0|.\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}|\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\frac{|\sin(|\xi|t)|}{|\xi|}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left(|\xi|t+\frac{|\sin(|\xi|t)|^{2}}{|\xi|}\right)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|.

Because of |ξ|​t​e−c0​|ξ|2​t≲1|\xi|\sqrt{t}\mathrm{e}^{-c_{0}|\xi|^{2}t}\lesssim 1 under c0∈(0,c)c_{0}\in(0,c) and boundedness of |sin⁡(|ξ|​t)||\sin(|\xi|t)|, the desired estimate (21) can be obtained. Similarly, we may get

χint​(ξ)|J^1k|≲χint​(ξ)​(1+|cos⁡(|ξ|​t)|)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|)+χint​(ξ)|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|e−c​|ξ|2​t​|θ^0|,\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}|\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left(1+|\cos(|\xi|t)|\right)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|\right)+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\sin(|\xi|t)|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|,

which leads to the first part of our estimate (22). Additionally, a direct subtraction implies

χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0−J^0k−J^1k|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}-\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}|
⩽χint​(ξ)​|−λR2​eλ1​t+(2​λR​λ1−λ12)​cos⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12​u^0k,p0|\displaystyle\qquad\leqslant\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left|\frac{-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{1}t}+(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{2})\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}}{2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2}}\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}\right|
+χint​(ξ)​|[λ1​(λR​λ1+λI2−λR2)+b2​|ξ|2​(λR−λ1)]​u^0k,p0+(λR2−λ12)​u^1k,p0λI​(2​λR​λ1−λI2−λR2−λ12)​sin⁡(λI​t)​eλR​t|\displaystyle\qquad\quad+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left|\frac{[\lambda_{1}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2})+b^{2}|\xi|^{2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}-\lambda_{1})]\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}+(\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}(2\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}^{2}-\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}-\lambda_{1}^{2})}\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{I}}t)\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}t}\right|
≲χint​(ξ)​(|ξ|2+|ξ|2​|cos⁡(|ξ|​t)|+|ξ|​|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​|u^0k,p0​|+χint​(ξ)|​ξ|​|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)​|e−c​|ξ|2​t|​u^1k,p0|\displaystyle\qquad\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left(|\xi|^{2}+|\xi|^{2}|\cos(|\xi|t)|+|\xi|\,|\sin(|\xi|t)|\right)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{0}|+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\xi|\,|\sin(|\xi|t)|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{1}|
≲χint​(ξ)​|ξ|​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|).\displaystyle\qquad\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\xi|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|\right).

To end the proof, we apply the triangle inequality resulting

χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0−J^0k|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}| ≲χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0−J^0k−J^1k|+χint​(ξ)​|J^1k|\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}-\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}|+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}|
≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|)\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right)

as well as

χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}| ≲χint​(ξ)​|u^k,p0−J^0k|+χint​(ξ)​|J^0k|\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}|+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}|
≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​|u^0k,p0|+χint​(ξ)​(1+t+|sin⁡(|ξ|​t)||ξ|)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|).\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left(1+\sqrt{t}+\frac{|\sin(|\xi|t)|}{|\xi|}\right)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right).

Hence, we complete the proof of this proposition. ∎

By ignoring the higher-order terms in the auxiliary function J^0k\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}, we may introduce two Fourier multipliers 𝒢^0=𝒢^0​(t,|ξ|)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0}(t,|\xi|) and 𝒢^1,k=𝒢^1,k​(t,ξ)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}(t,\xi) as follows:

𝒢^0\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0} :=sin⁡(b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|​t)b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|​e−κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2​t,\displaystyle:=\frac{\sin(\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|t)}{\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}|\xi|^{2}t},
𝒢^1,k\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k} :=i​γ1​ξk(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2​(cos⁡(b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|​t)​e−κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2​t−e−κ​b2b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|2​t),\displaystyle:=\frac{i\gamma_{1}\xi_{k}}{(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})|\xi|^{2}}\left(\cos\left(\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|t\right)\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}|\xi|^{2}t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa b^{2}}{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|^{2}t}\right),

which are the Fourier transforms of (12) and (13), respectively. Therefore, we can derive some approximations in the sense of additional factors |ξ|s|\xi|^{s} by subtracting some Fourier multipliers in the estimate comparing with the one in (21).

Proposition 3.3.

Concerning ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), the following estimates for some approximations hold:

χint​(ξ)​|J^0k−𝒢^0​u^1k,p0−𝒢^1,k​θ^0|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left|\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}-\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}\widehat{\theta}_{0}\right| ≲χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|),\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right), (24)
χint​(ξ)​|J^0k−(𝒢^0+ℋ^0)​u^1k,p0−(𝒢^1,k+ℋ^1,k)​θ^0|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left|\widehat{J}_{0}^{k}-(\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0}+\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{0})\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-(\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}+\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{1,k})\widehat{\theta}_{0}\right| ≲χint​(ξ)​|ξ|​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|),\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\xi|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right),

for any k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n, where ℋ^0=ℋ^0​(t,|ξ|)\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{0}=\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{0}(t,|\xi|) and ℋ^1,k=ℋ^1,k​(t,ξ)\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{1,k}=\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{1,k}(t,\xi) are defined by

ℋ^0\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{0} :=−κ2​γ1​γ2​(γ1​γ2+4​b2)8​(b2+γ1​γ2)3​|ξ|2​t​cos⁡(b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|​t)​e−κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2​t,\displaystyle:=-\frac{\kappa^{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}+4b^{2})}{8(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})^{3}}|\xi|^{2}t\cos\left(\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|t\right)\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}|\xi|^{2}t},

Secondly, we employ the analogous ideas as the treatment of J^0k\widehat{J}_{0}^{k} and denote 𝒢^2=𝒢^2​(t,|ξ|)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{2}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{2}(t,|\xi|), 𝒢^3=𝒢^3​(t,|ξ|)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{3}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{3}(t,|\xi|) and 𝒢^4,k=𝒢^4,k​(t,ξ)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{4,k}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{4,k}(t,\xi) by

𝒢^2\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{2} :=γ1​γ2b2+γ1​γ2​e−κ​b2b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|2​t+b2b2+γ1​γ2​cos⁡(b2+γ1​γ2​|ξ|​t)​e−κ​γ1​γ22​(b2+γ1​γ2)​|ξ|2​t,\displaystyle:=\frac{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa b^{2}}{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|^{2}t}+\frac{b^{2}}{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}\cos\left(\sqrt{b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}|\xi|t\right)\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\kappa\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}{2(b^{2}+\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})}|\xi|^{2}t},

Following the proof of the first estimate in Proposition 3.3, we can obtain the next result. Since the method of the demonstration is the same with slight changes of procedure, we omit the proof.

Proposition 3.4.

Concerning ξ∈𝒵int​(ε0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\intt}(\varepsilon_{0}), the following estimate for an approximation holds:

χint​(ξ)​|J^1k−𝒢^2​u^0k,p0−𝒢^3​u^1k,p0−𝒢^4,k​θ^0|\displaystyle\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\left|\widehat{J}_{1}^{k}-\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{2}\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{3}\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{4,k}\widehat{\theta}_{0}\right| ≲χint​(ξ)​|ξ|​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|)\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\intt}(\xi)|\xi|\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right)

for any k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n.

Eventually, to finish this subsection, we propose pointwise estimates localizing in bounded and large frequencies zones. They will not influence on large-time behaviors since exponential decays.

Proposition 3.5.

Concerning ξ∈𝒵bdd​(ε0,N0)∪𝒵ext​(N0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\bdd}(\varepsilon_{0},N_{0})\cup\mathcal{Z}_{\extt}(N_{0}), the following pointwise estimate holds:

(χbdd​(ξ)+χext​(ξ))​|u^k,p0|≲(χbdd​(ξ)+χext​(ξ))​e−c​t​(|u^0k,p0|+1⟨ξ⟩​|u^1k,p0|+1⟨ξ⟩2​|θ^0|)\displaystyle\big(\chi_{\bdd}(\xi)+\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\big)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}|\lesssim\big(\chi_{\bdd}(\xi)+\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\big)\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+\frac{1}{\langle\xi\rangle}|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+\frac{1}{\langle\xi\rangle^{2}}|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right)

for any k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n.

Proof.

Taking consideration of Proposition 3.1 as ξ∈𝒵ext​(N0)\xi\in\mathcal{Z}_{\extt}(N_{0}) in the representation (20), we are able to estimate

χext​(ξ)​|u^k,p0|\displaystyle\chi_{\extt}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}| ≲χext​(ξ)​(1|ξ|2​e−c​|ξ|2​t+e−c​t)​|u^0k,p0|+χext​(ξ)​(1|ξ|4​e−c​|ξ|2​t+1|ξ|​e−c​t)​|u^1k,p0|\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}+\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\right)|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{|\xi|^{4}}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}+\frac{1}{|\xi|}\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\right)|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|
+χext​(ξ)​(1|ξ|3​e−c​|ξ|2​t+1|ξ|2​e−c​t)​|θ^0|\displaystyle\quad+\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{|\xi|^{3}}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}+\frac{1}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\right)|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|
≲χext​(ξ)​e−c​t​(|u^0k,p0|+1|ξ|​|u^1k,p0|+1|ξ|2​|θ^0|).\displaystyle\lesssim\chi_{\extt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+\frac{1}{|\xi|}|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+\frac{1}{|\xi|^{2}}|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right).

For another, the last conclusion in Proposition 3.1 tells us that the solution in the Fourier space decays exponentially such that

χbdd​(ξ)​|u^k,p0|≲χbdd​(ξ)​e−c​t​(|u^0k,p0|+|u^1k,p0|+|θ^0|).\displaystyle\chi_{\bdd}(\xi)|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}|\lesssim\chi_{\bdd}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-ct}\left(|\widehat{u}_{0}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{u}_{1}^{k,p_{0}}|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}|\right).

The combination of previous two estimates and |ξ|≃⟨ξ⟩|\xi|\simeq\langle\xi\rangle for any |ξ|⩾ε0|\xi|\geqslant\varepsilon_{0} completes the proof. ∎

4 Large-time asymptotic profiles for the potential solution

The schedule of this section is arranged by: in Subsection 4.1, we will derive upper bound estimates and optimal lower bound estimates (8) for any physical dimensions n=1,2,3n=1,2,3; in Subsection 4.2, some estimates for the second-order profiles will be deduced; and finally in Subsection 4.3, the optimal leading terms will be investigated.

4.1 Optimal estimates and first-order profiles for the potential solution

This part contributes to the proof of Theorem 2.1. The second estimate in Proposition 3.2 shows

‖χint​(ξ)​u^k,p0​(t,ξ)‖L2\displaystyle\|\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}(t,\xi)\|_{L^{2}} ≲‖χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​|u^0k,p0​(ξ)|‖L2+(1+t)12​‖χint​(ξ)​e−c​|ξ|2​t​(|u^1k,p0​(ξ)|+|θ^0​(ξ)|)‖L2\displaystyle\lesssim\left\|\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{0}(\xi)|\right\|_{L^{2}}+(1+t)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\left(|\widehat{u}^{k,p_{0}}_{1}(\xi)|+|\widehat{\theta}_{0}(\xi)|\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}

for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 and any t≫1t\gg 1. Due to the situation that 𝒢^1,k​(t,ξ)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}(t,\xi) is not radial symmetric with respect to ξ\xi, we will frequently use the following chain for treating the multipliers ℳ⁡(|ξ|)\mathcal{M}(|\xi|) containing Riesz transform:

‖ℛk​ℳ^​(|ξ|)‖L22=∫ℝ⋉|ℳ^​(|ξ|)|2​ξk2|ξ|2​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mathcal{R}_{k}\mathcal{M}}(|\xi|)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\widehat{\mathcal{M}}(|\xi|)|^{2}\frac{\xi_{k}^{2}}{|\xi|^{2}}\mathrm{d}\xi =∫0∞|ℳ^​(r)|2​rn−1​𝑑r​∫𝕊⋉−⊮ωk2​d​σω\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}|\widehat{\mathcal{M}}(r)|^{2}r^{n-1}\mathrm{d}r\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\omega_{k}^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}

Proposition 4.1.

Let us take any βj>0\beta_{j}>0 for j=0,1,2j=0,1,2. Concerning the Fourier multiplier

ℳn​(t,|ξ|):=1|ξ|​(e−β0​|ξ|2​t−cos⁡(β1​|ξ|​t)​e−β2​|ξ|2​t),\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|):=\frac{1}{|\xi|}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{0}|\xi|^{2}t}-\cos(\beta_{1}|\xi|t)\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\right),

the following optimal estimates hold:

‖ℳn​(t,|ξ|)‖L2≃𝒜n​(t)\displaystyle\|\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq\mathcal{A}_{n}(t) (34)

for any n=1,2,3n=1,2,3 and t≫1t\gg 1.

Proof.

Thanks to exponential decay estimates when |ξ|⩾ε0|\xi|\geqslant\varepsilon_{0}, the upper bound estimates (34) have been finished actually at the beginning of this subsection due to the trick (23), boundedness of since functions and (27). For these reasons, we just need to concentrate on (34) from the below side, which is the most challenging part in the optimal estimates. To do so, we will separate our discussion into three parts in terms of dimensions.

Lower-dimensional case: n=1n=1. With the same philosophy as those in (23), in general we may rewrite the multiplier by

ℳn​(t,|ξ|)=2|ξ|​|sin⁡(β12​|ξ|​t)|2​e−β2​|ξ|2​t+(β2−β0)​|ξ|​t​e−β2​|ξ|2​t​∫01e(β2−β0)​|ξ|2​t​s​𝑑s.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|)=\frac{2}{|\xi|}\left|\sin\left(\tfrac{\beta_{1}}{2}|\xi|t\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}+(\beta_{2}-\beta_{0})|\xi|t\mathrm{e}^{-\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{(\beta_{2}-\beta_{0})|\xi|^{2}ts}\mathrm{d}s.

Note that the last term in the above will vanish when β0=β2\beta_{0}=\beta_{2}. Hence, we apply 2​|f−g|2⩾|f|2−2​|g|22|f-g|^{2}\geqslant|f|^{2}-2|g|^{2} to deduce

‖ℳn​(t,|ξ|)‖L22\displaystyle\|\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|)\|_{L^{2}}^{2} ⩾‖χint​(ξ)​ℳn​(t,|ξ|)‖L22\displaystyle\geqslant\|\chi_{\intt}(\xi)\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
⩾∫|ξ|⩽ε02|ξ|2​|sin⁡(β12​|ξ|​t)|4​e−2​β2​|ξ|2​t​𝑑ξ−C​t2​∫|ξ|⩽ε0|ξ|2​e−c​|ξ|2​t​𝑑ξ.\displaystyle\geqslant\int_{|\xi|\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{2}{|\xi|^{2}}\left|\sin\left(\tfrac{\beta_{1}}{2}|\xi|t\right)\right|^{4}\mathrm{e}^{-2\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\mathrm{d}\xi-Ct^{2}\int_{|\xi|\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}}|\xi|^{2}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\mathrm{d}\xi.

|sin⁡(β12​|ξ|​t)|⩾C>0for any|ξ|∈[α0​t−1,2​α0​t−1].\displaystyle\left|\sin\left(\tfrac{\beta_{1}}{2}|\xi|t\right)\right|\geqslant C>0\ \ \mbox{for any}\ \ |\xi|\in[\alpha_{0}t^{-1},2\alpha_{0}t^{-1}].

We take large-time t≫1t\gg 1 so that 2​α0​t−1<ε02\alpha_{0}t^{-1}<\varepsilon_{0} always holds. Thus, we shrank the domain of the first integral only and derive

‖ℳn​(t,|ξ|)‖L22\displaystyle\|\mathcal{M}_{n}(t,|\xi|)\|_{L^{2}}^{2} ⩾∫α0​t−1⩽|ξ|⩽2​α0​t−12|ξ|2​|sin⁡(β12​|ξ|​t)|4​e−2​β2​|ξ|2​t​𝑑ξ−C​t​∫|ξ|⩽ε0e−c​|ξ|2​t​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\geqslant\int_{\alpha_{0}t^{-1}\leqslant|\xi|\leqslant 2\alpha_{0}t^{-1}}\frac{2}{|\xi|^{2}}\left|\sin\left(\tfrac{\beta_{1}}{2}|\xi|t\right)\right|^{4}\mathrm{e}^{-2\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\mathrm{d}\xi-Ct\int_{|\xi|\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}}\mathrm{e}^{-c|\xi|^{2}t}\mathrm{d}\xi
≳t2​∫α0​t−1⩽|ξ|⩽2​α0​t−1e−2​β2​|ξ|2​t​𝑑ξ−C​t1−n2\displaystyle\gtrsim t^{2}\int_{\alpha_{0}t^{-1}\leqslant|\xi|\leqslant 2\alpha_{0}t^{-1}}\mathrm{e}^{-2\beta_{2}|\xi|^{2}t}\mathrm{d}\xi-Ct^{1-\frac{n}{2}}

≳t2−n\displaystyle\gtrsim t^{2-n}

for n=1,2n=1,2 and t≫1t\gg 1, where we used (26). Nevertheless, considering n=2n=2, the last lower bound is just a constant which seems to be not sharp. For this reason, we will employ another idea in such critical-dimension.

Critical-dimensional case: n=2n=2. By considering polar coordinates and shrinking the resultant domain into [t−12,1][t^{-\frac{1}{2}},1] for t≫1t\gg 1, one may see

4.2 Second-order asymptotic profiles for the potential solution

Firstly, let us explain shortly the idea of construction for the second-order profile ψk=ψk​(t,x)\psi^{k}=\psi^{k}(t,x) since the first-order profile (leading term) φk=φk​(t,x)\varphi^{k}=\varphi^{k}(t,x) has been built by extracting the dominant terms. To get the second-order profile, we not only derive the second-order expansions of solution, but also need to find the worst term with the help of Taylor’s expansions. Recalling the profiles φk​(t,x)\varphi^{k}(t,x) and ψk​(t,x)\psi^{k}(t,x), we apply a suitable decomposition as follows:

uk,p0​(t,x)−φk​(t,x)−ψk​(t,x)=∑j=1,…,6ℰj​(t,x),\displaystyle u^{k,p_{0}}(t,x)-\varphi^{k}(t,x)-\psi^{k}(t,x)=\sum\limits_{j=1,\dots,6}\mathcal{E}_{j}(t,x),

where these error functions are defined by

and

ℰ2​(t,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{2}(t,x) :=𝒢0​(t,|D|)​u1k,p0−𝒢0​(t,x)​Pu1k,p0−∇𝒢0​(t,x)∘Mu1k,p0,\displaystyle:=\mathcal{G}_{0}(t,|D|)u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-\mathcal{G}_{0}(t,x)P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}-\nabla\mathcal{G}_{0}(t,x)\circ M_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}},
ℰ3​(t,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{3}(t,x) :=𝒢1,k​(t,D)​θ0−𝒢1,k​(t,x)​Pθ0−∇𝒢1,k​(t,x)∘Mθ0,\displaystyle:=\mathcal{G}_{1,k}(t,D)\theta_{0}-\mathcal{G}_{1,k}(t,x)P_{\theta_{0}}-\nabla\mathcal{G}_{1,k}(t,x)\circ M_{\theta_{0}},

ℰ4​(t,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{4}(t,x) :=𝒢2​(t,|D|)​u0k,p0−𝒢2​(t,x)​Pu0k,p0,\displaystyle:=\mathcal{G}_{2}(t,|D|)u_{0}^{k,p_{0}}-\mathcal{G}_{2}(t,x)P_{u_{0}^{k,p_{0}}},
ℰ5​(t,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{5}(t,x) :=(ℋ0​(t,|D|)+𝒢3​(t,|D|))​u1k,p0−(ℋ0​(t,x)+𝒢3​(t,x))​Pu1k,p0,\displaystyle:=\big(\mathcal{H}_{0}(t,|D|)+\mathcal{G}_{3}(t,|D|)\big)u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}-\big(\mathcal{H}_{0}(t,x)+\mathcal{G}_{3}(t,x)\big)P_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}},
ℰ6​(t,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{6}(t,x) :=(ℋ1,k​(t,D)+𝒢4,k​(t,D))​θ0−(ℋ1,k​(t,x)+𝒢4,k​(t,x))​Pθ0.\displaystyle:=\big(\mathcal{H}_{1,k}(t,D)+\mathcal{G}_{4,k}(t,D)\big)\theta_{0}-\big(\mathcal{H}_{1,k}(t,x)+\mathcal{G}_{4,k}(t,x)\big)P_{\theta_{0}}.

for t≫1t\gg 1. To deal with the second error term, we may decompose it into three functions as follows:

carrying a small positive constant α1≪1\alpha_{1}\ll 1. The application of Taylor’s expansions implies

4.3 Optimal estimates for the leading term

Concerning upper bound estimates for large-time, we have proved them already in (29) and (30) totally. Thus, we are just required to concentrate on the lower one, whose key is lower bound estimates for ψk​(t,⋅)\psi^{k}(t,\cdot) in the L2L^{2} norm. The Fourier imagine of ψk​(t,⋅)\psi^{k}(t,\cdot) is represented by

ψ^k​(t,ξ)\displaystyle\widehat{\psi}^{k}(t,\xi) =i⁡((ξ∘Mu1k,p0)​𝒢^0​(t,|ξ|)+(ξ∘Mθ0)​𝒢^1,k​(t,ξ))+𝒢^2​(t,|ξ|)​Pu0k,p0\displaystyle=i\left(\big(\xi\circ M_{u_{1}^{k,p_{0}}}\big)\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{0}(t,|\xi|)+(\xi\circ M_{\theta_{0}})\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{1,k}(t,\xi)\right)+\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{2}(t,|\xi|)P_{u_{0}^{k,p_{0}}}

for t≫1t\gg 1. Then, we complete the proof of Theorem 2.2.

5 Final remarks

Throughout this work, we have investigated large-time asymptotic profiles for a typical hyperbolic-parabolic coupled system, i.e. the classical thermoelastic system for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3. Our methods are based on the treatments for third-order (in time) evolution equations and fine analyses for the Fourier multipliers carrying singularities, dissipations and oscillations. We conjecture that our methodology can be generalized to other thermoelastic models even hyperbolic-hyperbolic coupled systems, including thermoelasticity system with second sound [21, 22] (i.e. elastic body with Cattaneo’s law of heat conduction), thermoelasticity of type II or type III [26, 29] (i.e. elastic body with Jeffreys type of heat conduction). Nevertheless, one needs a suitable way to deal with fourth-order evolution equations.

Appendix A Lower bound estimates for the free wave equation

This appendix contributes to lower bound estimates of the solution to the linear wave model (10) under w1∈L1w_{1}\in L^{1} regularity, which improves the estimates in [7, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2]. To be specific, we only require L1L^{1} regularity rather than L1,1L^{1,1} regularity in [7] for the second data. Moreover, we do not rely on the trick of shrinking domain in [7, Equation (2.17)].

The crucial tool is estimating the oscillating Fourier multiplier in the next proposition.

Proposition A.1.

Let g∈L1g\in L^{1} for n=1,2n=1,2. The following lower bound estimates hold:

Ig​(t,n):=‖ℱξ→x−1​(sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|ξ|​g^​(ξ))‖L2≳{t​|Pg|ifn=1,ln⁡t​|Pg|ifn=2,\displaystyle I_{g}(t;n):=\left\|\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}\left(\frac{\sin(|\xi|t)}{|\xi|}\widehat{g}(\xi)\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}\gtrsim\begin{cases}\sqrt{t}\,|P_{g}|&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \sqrt{\ln t}\,|P_{g}|&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\end{cases}

for any t≫1t\gg 1.

Proof.

When n=1n=1, the application of change of variable η=ξ​t\eta=\xi t shows

(Ig​(t,1))2=t​∫ℝ|sin⁡η|2|η|2​|g^​(t−1​η)|2​𝑑η.\displaystyle\big(I_{g}(t;1)\big)^{2}=t\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-1}\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta. (44)

By the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and g^​(0)=Pg\widehat{g}(0)=P_{g}, we know

limt→∞∫ℝ|sin⁡η|2|η|2​|g^​(t−1​η)|2​𝑑η\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-1}\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta =∫ℝ|sin⁡η|2|η|2​|g^​(0)|2​𝑑η=|Pg|∫ℝ2⁡|sin⁡η|2|η|2​𝑑η,\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}|\widehat{g}(0)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta=|P_{g}|^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\mathrm{d}\eta,

namely,

∫ℝ|sin⁡η|2|η|2​|g^​(t−1​η)|2​𝑑η−|Pg|2​∫ℝ|sin⁡η|2|η|2​𝑑η=o⁡(1)\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-1}\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta-|P_{g}|^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\mathrm{d}\eta=o(1)

for t≫1t\gg 1. So, one can get

RHS of (44)=t|Pg|∫ℝ2⁡|sin⁡η|2|η|2​𝑑η+o⁡(t)≳t​|Pg|2\displaystyle\mbox{RHS of \eqref{Eq-*1}}=t|P_{g}|^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|\sin\eta|^{2}}{|\eta|^{2}}\mathrm{d}\eta+o(t)\gtrsim t|P_{g}|^{2}

for t≫1t\gg 1, due to the fact that ∫ℝ|η|−2​|sin⁡η|2​𝑑η\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\eta|^{-2}|\sin\eta|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta is a positive constant.

For the case in the two-dimension n=2n=2, we apply polar coordinates and η=t​r\eta=\sqrt{t}r to find

(Ig​(t,2))2\displaystyle\big(I_{g}(t;2)\big)^{2} =∫0∞|sin⁡(r​t)|2r​∫𝕊|g^​(ω​r)|2​d​σω​𝑑r\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{|\sin(rt)|^{2}}{r}\int_{\mathbb{S}}|\widehat{g}(\omega r)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}\mathrm{d}r
⩾∫0∞e−r2​t​|sin⁡(r​t)|2r​∫𝕊|g^​(ω​r)|2​d​σω​𝑑r\displaystyle\geqslant\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-r^{2}t}\frac{|\sin(rt)|^{2}}{r}\int_{\mathbb{S}}|\widehat{g}(\omega r)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}\mathrm{d}r
⩾∫0∞e−η2​|sin⁡(t​η)|2η​∫𝕊|g^​(t−12​ω​η)|2​d​σω​𝑑η,\displaystyle\geqslant\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{|\sin(\sqrt{t}\eta)|^{2}}{\eta}\int_{\mathbb{S}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\omega\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}\mathrm{d}\eta, (45)

where we considered e−r2​t⩽1\mathrm{e}^{-r^{2}t}\leqslant 1 for any t⩾0t\geqslant 0. Again, employing the well-known Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and g^​(0)=Pg\widehat{g}(0)=P_{g}, it holds

limt→∞∫𝕊|g^​(t−12​ω​η)|2​d​σω=∫𝕊|g^​(0)|2​d​σω=|Pg|2​|𝕊|,\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{S}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\omega\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}=\int_{\mathbb{S}}|\widehat{g}(0)|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}=|P_{g}|^{2}|\mathbb{S}|,

∫𝕊|g^​(t−12​ω​η)|2​d​σω⩾12​|Pg|2​|𝕊|.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}}\left|\widehat{g}\left(t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\omega\eta\right)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\omega}\geqslant\frac{1}{2}|P_{g}|^{2}|\mathbb{S}|.

Consequently, the shrinking of domain into [t−12,1][t^{-\frac{1}{2}},1] implies

RHS of (45) ⩾12|Pg|2|𝕊|∫≈−⊮⊭⊮−η⊭|sin⁡(≈​η)|⊭ηη\displaystyle\geqslant\frac{1}{2}|P_{g}|^{2}|\mathbb{S}|\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{|\sin(\sqrt{t}\eta)|^{2}}{\eta}\mathrm{}\eta
=14|Pg|2|𝕊|(∫≈−⊮⊭⊮−η⊭⊮ηη−∫≈−⊮⊭⊮−η⊭cos⁡(⊭​≈​η)ηη).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}|P_{g}|^{2}|\mathbb{S}|\left(\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{1}{\eta}\mathrm{}\eta-\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{\cos(2\sqrt{t}\eta)}{\eta}\mathrm{}\eta\right).

For one thing, a direct consequence indicates

∫t−121e−η2​1η​𝑑η⩾e−1​∫t−1211η​𝑑η=12​e​ln⁡t\displaystyle\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{1}{\eta}\mathrm{d}\eta\geqslant\mathrm{e}^{-1}\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\frac{1}{\eta}\mathrm{d}\eta=\frac{1}{2\mathrm{e}}\ln t

for t≫1t\gg 1, and an integration by parts leads to

∫t−121e−η2​cos⁡(2​t​η)η​𝑑η=(e−η2​sin⁡(2​t​η)2​t​η)|η=t−12η=1+∫t−121sin⁡(2​t​η)2​t​e−η2​(2+1η2)​𝑑η.\displaystyle\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{\cos(2\sqrt{t}\eta)}{\eta}\mathrm{d}\eta=\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{\sin(2\sqrt{t}\eta)}{2\sqrt{t}\eta}\right)\Big|_{\eta=t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{\eta=1}+\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\frac{\sin(2\sqrt{t}\eta)}{2\sqrt{t}}\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\left(2+\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}\eta.

It immediately gives

|∫t−121e−η2​cos⁡(2​t​η)η​𝑑η|⩽1t+1+1t​∫01𝑑η+12​t​∫t−121η−2​𝑑η≲1\displaystyle\left|\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{-\eta^{2}}\frac{\cos(2\sqrt{t}\eta)}{\eta}\mathrm{d}\eta\right|\leqslant\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}\eta+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\int_{t^{-\frac{1}{2}}}^{1}\eta^{-2}\mathrm{d}\eta\lesssim 1

RHS of (45)≳ln⁡t​|Pg|2−c≳ln⁡t​|Pg|2\displaystyle\mbox{RHS of \eqref{Eq-*2}}\gtrsim\ln t\,|P_{g}|^{2}-c\gtrsim\ln t\,|P_{g}|^{2}

for t≫1t\gg 1, which demonstrates the desired estimate for n=2n=2. ∎

Corollary A.1.

Let us consider the free wave equation (10) for n=1,2n=1,2 carrying initial datum w0∈L2w_{0}\in L^{2} and w1∈L1w_{1}\in L^{1}. Then, the solution ww satisfies the following lower bound estimates:

‖w⁡(t,⋅)‖L2≳{t​|Pw1|ifn=1,ln⁡t​|Pw1|ifn=2,\displaystyle\|w(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\gtrsim\begin{cases}\sqrt{t}\,|P_{w_{1}}|&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \sqrt{\ln t}\,|P_{w_{1}}|&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\end{cases}

for any t≫1t\gg 1.

Remark A.1.

This result implies that the solution of free wave equation grows to infinite as t→∞t\to\infty providing that |Pw1|≠0|P_{w_{1}}|\neq 0. Due to the upper bound estimates in [7], we may state the optimal growth estimates ‖w⁡(t,⋅)‖L2≃𝒜n​(t)\|w(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}}\simeq\mathcal{A}_{n}(t) for t≫1t\gg 1 and n=1,2n=1,2 by taking initial datum in L2∩L1L^{2}\cap L^{1} and |Pw1|≠0|P_{w_{1}}|\neq 0.

Proof.

It is well-known that the solution of (10) in the Fourier space is expressed by

w^=cos⁡(|ξ|​t)​w^0+sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|ξ|​w^1.\displaystyle\widehat{w}=\cos(|\xi|t)\widehat{w}_{0}+\frac{\sin(|\xi|t)}{|\xi|}\widehat{w}_{1}.

Hence, according to 2​|f+g|2⩾|f|2−2​|g|22|f+g|^{2}\geqslant|f|^{2}-2|g|^{2} and Proposition A.1, we get

‖w^​(t,ξ)‖L22\displaystyle\|\widehat{w}(t,\xi)\|_{L^{2}}^{2} ⩾12​‖ℱξ→x−1​(sin⁡(|ξ|​t)|ξ|​w^1)‖L22−‖ℱξ→x−1​(cos⁡(|ξ|​t)​w^0)‖L22\displaystyle\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}\left(\frac{\sin(|\xi|t)}{|\xi|}\widehat{w}_{1}\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}-\left\|\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\xi\to x}\big(\cos(|\xi|t)\widehat{w}_{0}\big)\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
≳{t​|Pw1|2−‖w0‖L22ifn=1,ln⁡t​|Pw1|2−‖w0‖L22ifn=2,\displaystyle\gtrsim\begin{cases}t|P_{w_{1}}|^{2}-\|w_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=1,\\ \ln t\,|P_{w_{1}}|^{2}-\|w_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&\mbox{if}\ \ n=2,\end{cases}

for t≫1t\gg 1. Because of w0∈L2w_{0}\in L^{2} as well as w1∈L1w_{1}\in L^{1}, our proof is completed. ∎
